Thailand.fee: The region's worst: a flat 220 ฿ (~$6) surcharge on every foreign-card withdrawal, at every bank. Soften it by withdrawing the max (20,000–30,000 ฿) in one go.
Thailand.lim: 20,000–30,000 ฿ per pull (Krungsri and CIMB sit at the generous end) — max it out to dilute that flat fee.
Thailand.tip: Thailand is an EXCHANGE country: bring crisp USD/EUR notes and change at SuperRich (the green/orange booths) or Vasu in Bangkok — rates beat any card path. Counter cash-advance inside a bank branch (passport needed) also dodges the 220 ฿.

Malaysia.fee: Kind by comparison: most local banks add no surcharge, or a small RM 10–12 at worst — only your home bank's fees apply.
Malaysia.lim: Typically RM 1,500–3,000 per pull, some machines RM 5,000.
Malaysia.tip: Licensed money changers (malls in KL, Lebuh Chulia in George Town) give excellent cash rates for major currencies — fine for topping up, no need to carry big sums.

Vietnam.fee: Typically 22,000–55,000 ₫ per withdrawal with lowish limits (2–5 M ₫); TPBank and VPBank are the traveller favourites for free or near-free pulls with higher limits.
Vietnam.lim: Most banks 2–5 M ₫ per pull; TPBank and VPBank allow up to ~8–10 M ₫ — another reason they're the picks.
Vietnam.tip: Cards are fine, but exchange counters at banks or gold shops give honest rates for USD/EUR. Refuse any ATM's own 'conversion' — always be charged in đồng.

Indonesia.fee: Most big-bank ATMs add no local surcharge — your bank's fee is the whole cost. Limits per pull are modest (2.5 M Rp on 50k-note machines).
Indonesia.lim: 1.25–2.5 M Rp on 50k-note machines; look for 100k-note machines (marked on the slot) for ~3 M Rp pulls.
Indonesia.tip: Use ATMs attached to real bank branches, never lone boxes in tourist lanes. On Gili Air, machines run dry and offline — carry cash over from Bali/Lombok. Exchange only at authorised 'PVA Berizin' offices; street 'no commission' boards are sleight-of-hand counters.

Philippines.fee: A flat ₱250 rides on almost every foreign withdrawal, with 10,000–20,000 ₱ limits — it stings in percentages on small pulls.
Philippines.lim: ₱10,000–20,000 at most banks; HSBC allows up to ₱40,000 — four fees become one.
Philippines.tip: HSBC branches allow bigger single withdrawals, diluting the flat fee. Bring some USD as backup for islands; change at bank counters or established changers, not kiosks.

North Macedonia.fee: Local bank ATMs are generally surcharge-free — only your home bank's cut applies.
North Macedonia.lim: Around 20,000–30,000 ден per pull at most banks — generous relative to prices here.
North Macedonia.tip: This is an exchange-friendly country: menuvachnici (exchange offices) convert EUR cash at razor-thin spreads — arriving with euros and changing as you go is genuinely the cheapest path.

Serbia.fee: Bank ATMs mostly add nothing; the plague is Euronet's blue boxes with painful rates and fees — walk past every one.
Serbia.lim: Commonly 40,000–60,000 din per pull at bank machines.
Serbia.tip: Menjačnice (exchange offices) are everywhere and excellent — EUR cash changes at near-interbank rates in Belgrade. Always pay and withdraw in dinars, never accept conversion.

Montenegro.fee: It's euro country, and most banks here do surcharge foreign cards ~€2–4 per withdrawal.
Montenegro.tip: Simplest play: arrive with EUR cash — it's the local currency, so no exchange needed at all. Withdraw rarely and large when you must.

Czechia.fee: Czech bank ATMs are surcharge-free; Euronet's tourist-zone army is not — and its 'converted' rates are 10 %+ bad.
Czechia.lim: Bank machines allow hefty pulls (10,000–20,000+ Kč); Euronet deliberately caps low to multiply its fees.
Czechia.tip: Never touch the Old-Town exchange kiosks with the '0 % commission' signs — the margin is in the rate. If you must change cash, use a bank or a vetted honest exchange; otherwise card + bank ATM is perfect. Decline CZK↔your-currency 'conversion' every single time.

Slovakia.fee: Eurozone: bank ATMs add no surcharge; only Euronet boxes do.
Slovakia.lim: Typically €300–700 per pull at bank machines.
Slovakia.tip: Cards work everywhere; keep a €20 note for markets and you're covered.

Romania.fee: Bank ATMs are broadly surcharge-free; the Old-Town Euronet boxes are the trap, as ever.
Romania.lim: Bank machines 2,000–5,000 lei; Euronet caps around 800 to farm fees.
Romania.tip: Withdraw lei from bank machines and always in lei. For cash exchange use banks or established case de schimb — never the guy 'helping' near a machine.

Poland.fee: Bank ATMs: no surcharge. Euronet: everywhere, and to be avoided everywhere.
Poland.lim: Bank machines 1,000–3,000+ zł; Euronet again caps low on purpose.
Poland.tip: Poland is also a good exchange country: kantors (away from stations and tourist squares) change EUR/USD at tight spreads. Pay in złoty always — DCC is the national tourist tax.

Estonia.fee: Surcharge-free bank ATMs — though you'll barely need cash in Europe's most card-native country.
Estonia.lim: Machine ceilings of €500–1,000+ — effectively your own card's daily limit.
Estonia.tip: Skip exchanging entirely; tap your card for everything from markets to trams.

Latvia.fee: Same story: bank ATMs free of local fees, cash barely needed.
Latvia.lim: Same: €500–1,000+ ceilings, your card's limit is the real cap.
Latvia.tip: Card everywhere; a little cash for Central Market stalls is all you'll want.

Italy.fee: Bank 'bancomat' machines add no local surcharge; independent boxes (Euronet and friends) at stations and sights do.
Italy.tip: Withdraw at real bank branches, always in euros. Skip airport/tourist exchange counters entirely — rates are ceremonial robbery.

France.fee: Bank ATMs ('distributeurs') are surcharge-free; avoid the gold-and-blue independent machines near sights.
France.tip: Card country; you need little cash. If exchanging, a bank beats every bureau on the tourist trail.

Belgium.fee: Bank ATMs (now often shared white 'CASH' points) are surcharge-free for standard withdrawals.
Belgium.tip: Frites stands take cards these days; keep a €10 note for markets and you're set.

United Kingdom.fee: Most bank and LINK machines are marked 'FREE cash withdrawals' — trust the label; convenience-store boxes charging £1.50–2 are the ones to skip.
United Kingdom.lim: Typically £300–500 per pull at bank machines.
United Kingdom.tip: Always charge in pounds, never the 'helpful' home-currency option. Exchange offices are unnecessary — the free ATM network wins.

Portugal.fee: The state Multibanco (MB) network adds no surcharge (€200/withdrawal, €400/day). Euronet paints its Lisbon boxes to look like MB — check the logo.
Portugal.lim: The Multibanco rule: €200 per withdrawal, €400 per day — plan around it.
Portugal.tip: Real Multibanco + paying in euros = zero drama. Tourist-strip exchange counters exist only for the unwary.

Spain.fee: The tricky one: Spanish banks surcharge foreign cards €0–5 each — Santander and CaixaBank sit at the punchy end, smaller banks are kind.
Spain.lim: €300–600 typical; some machines offer €1,000 'premium' pulls with a bigger fee — decline.
Spain.tip: Check the on-screen fee before confirming and walk to the next bank if it's €3+. Decline conversion, and skip exchange offices — a low-fee ATM beats them all.

Norway.fee: Minibank ATMs are surcharge-free — but this is a near-cashless country; you may go the whole trip without notes.
Norway.lim: 5,000–10,000 kr per pull (9,900 is a common ceiling) — not that you'll need it.
Norway.tip: Don't exchange money for Norway at all. Card and phone cover 100 % of life; a single small withdrawal covers flea markets.

Sweden.fee: The blue cooperative 'Bankomat' machines are the standard and add nothing.
Sweden.lim: Bankomat machines allow 5,000–10,000 kr per pull.
Sweden.tip: Sweden is arguably the most cashless place on Earth — some cafés refuse cash. Don't exchange; just tap.

Finland.fee: Orange 'Otto.' machines are the national free network. The yellow 'Nosto' machines charge — learn the two names and you're done.
Finland.tip: Otto = yes, Nosto = no. Beyond that, card everything.

United States.fee: Every machine that isn't your own bank's charges $3–5.50, and hotel/store ATMs push $6+. There's no free-for-foreigners network.
United States.lim: Usually $300–800 per pull depending on the bank — your card's daily cap is often the binding limit.
United States.tip: Minimise cash entirely — the US runs on cards. If you need bills, one big withdrawal at a major bank branch ATM. Never use airport exchange counters; their rates are the worst in the country.

Dominican Republic.fee: Expect RD$200–350 per withdrawal with modest limits; resort-lobby machines charge most of all.
Dominican Republic.tip: USD cash is welcome nearly everywhere tourist-side — bring some. Change at banks or proper cambios; count carefully, smile always.

Egypt.fee: Most bank ATMs add little or nothing; the constraint is per-pull limits (3,000–4,000 E£ typically).
Egypt.lim: 3,000–4,000 E£ per pull is the norm; do several pulls on separate days for big spends.
Egypt.tip: Bring USD or EUR notes — bank exchange is quick and cash rules daily life here. Hoard small bills; everyone 'has no change'.

Mauritius.fee: MCB and SBM machines are low- or no-surcharge and everywhere that matters.
Mauritius.lim: Typically Rs 10,000–25,000 per pull at MCB/SBM.
Mauritius.tip: Bank exchange counters (even the airport ones) run fair spreads here — changing some EUR on arrival is perfectly fine.

Netherlands.fee: Bank ATMs (Geldmaat, the shared yellow network) add no surcharge — only your home bank's fee.
Netherlands.tip: Card and phone cover everything here; many places are cashless. Skip exchange offices entirely.

Austria.fee: Bank ATMs (Bankomat) are surcharge-free; Euronet boxes near sights are the trap.
Austria.tip: Pay in euros always. Vienna runs largely on cards; keep a €20 note for markets.

Hungary.fee: Bank ATMs add no surcharge, but many now ask a rendszerdíj — decline the on-screen fee and use a bank machine. Euronet is everywhere and awful.
Hungary.lim: Bank machines 150,000–300,000 Ft; Euronet caps low to farm fees.
Hungary.tip: Always pay and withdraw in forint, never euros — the 'conversion' is a 10% tax. Budapest has good exchange offices away from Váci utca.

Greece.fee: Greek bank ATMs surcharge foreign cards €2–3; Euronet's island armies charge more with worse rates.
Greece.tip: On islands, withdraw enough in town — remote machines run dry in August. Decline conversion; skip Euronet.

Croatia.fee: Now euro country; bank ATMs are surcharge-free, Euronet boxes in Dubrovnik/Split old towns are not.
Croatia.tip: Avoid the tourist-zone Euronet machines and their 'conversion'. Bank machines + euros = no drama.

Germany.fee: Bank ATMs (Sparkasse, Volksbank, the big four) are surcharge-free; independent boxes charge €4–6.
Germany.tip: Germany still loves cash — carry more than you'd expect; some Berlin bars and bakeries are cash-only. Bank ATMs, always.

Ireland.fee: Bank ATMs are free for withdrawals; convenience-store machines may charge.
Ireland.tip: Charge in euros, never the home-currency option. Cards work everywhere; little cash needed.

Denmark.fee: Bank ATMs are surcharge-free — but Denmark is nearly cashless, so you may never use one.
Denmark.tip: Don't exchange money; MobilePay and cards run the country. A single small withdrawal covers flea markets.

Iceland.fee: Bank ATMs (Landsbankinn, Íslandsbanki, Arion) are surcharge-free.
Iceland.lim: Effectively your card's daily limit — high ceilings.
Iceland.tip: Iceland is the most cashless country you'll visit — cards work at remote petrol pumps and hot dog stands alike. Barely withdraw at all.

Switzerland.fee: Bank ATMs (UBS, PostFinance, cantonal banks) add no surcharge; watch machines that quote in your home currency.
Switzerland.tip: Everything's expensive, nothing's a scam. Pay in francs, decline conversion, and note many places take euros at a poor rate — francs win.

Mexico.fee: Most bank ATMs charge a surcharge (~$3–6); Santander, Banorte and Scotiabank are usually the kindest. Avoid standalone tourist-zone machines.
Mexico.lim: 5,000–9,000 MXN per pull at most banks (some offer up to 12,000).
Mexico.tip: Always withdraw in pesos and DECLINE the on-screen conversion. In tourist spots, use ATMs inside real bank branches, not the flashy 'no-fee' boxes in bars and lobbies (they gouge on the rate).

Cuba.fee: The system barely works for foreigners: many international cards (especially US-linked) are rejected, and ATMs are unreliable.
Cuba.lim: Low and inconsistent when they work at all.
Cuba.tip: Treat Cuba as cash-only: bring ALL the money you'll need in clean USD or EUR notes and exchange at official CADECA offices or your casa. Keep a reserve. Never rely on cards — plan the whole trip's budget in cash before you fly.

Guatemala.fee: Bank ATMs charge ~$3–4 per withdrawal; 5B and Banrural machines are widely available.
Guatemala.tip: Withdraw inside banks or malls, not on the street. Antigua and Panajachel have plenty of ATMs; carry some cash for villages and chicken-buses where cards are useless. Quetzales only — decline conversion.

Nicaragua.fee: ATMs charge ~$4–5 and can be scarce outside cities.
Nicaragua.lim: Often capped around 6,000–8,000 NIO per pull.
Nicaragua.tip: León and Managua have reliable bank ATMs (BAC is the most card-friendly). Carry enough córdobas/US cash for smaller towns; USD is often accepted. Withdraw in local currency and decline conversion.

Costa Rica.fee: Bank ATMs charge modest fees; machines dispense both colones and USD.
Costa Rica.lim: Usually ₡200,000 or a few hundred USD per pull.
Costa Rica.tip: Choose colones and DECLINE conversion. In remote surf towns (Santa Teresa!) ATMs are few and run dry on weekends — draw cash in a town with a bank branch before heading out. USD is widely accepted alongside colones.

Panama.fee: ATMs charge ~$5–6 (a 'Servicio Bancario' fee) on most withdrawals.
Panama.lim: Often capped low ($250–500) which stacks the flat fee — withdraw the max.
Panama.tip: Panama uses the US dollar (the 'balboa' is 1:1), so no exchange needed at all — just bring/withdraw USD. On Bocas islands, ATMs are few and can run out; carry enough cash over from the mainland.

Colombia.fee: Most bank ATMs charge ~$3–5; Davivienda, Bancolombia and BBVA are reliable. Servibanca often lets you skip the fee.
Colombia.lim: Bancolombia caps low (~600,000 COP); Davivienda and BBVA allow more per pull.
Colombia.tip: Withdraw inside malls or bank branches, cover the keypad, and take only what you need. Choose pesos, decline conversion. Medellín and Cartagena are full of ATMs; use the ones in guarded, indoor locations.

Venezuela.fee: The local banking system is effectively unusable for foreign cards, and hyperinflation makes bolívares impractical.
Venezuela.lim: Not a viable option for travellers.
Venezuela.tip: Venezuela runs on US dollars in cash now — bring clean, small-denomination USD notes and use them directly (widely accepted). Don't rely on ATMs or cards at all, don't flash cash, and change only tiny amounts to bolívares if ever needed. Cash discipline here is also a safety matter.

Ecuador.fee: ATMs charge ~$4–5; Banco Pichincha and Banco Guayaquil are the widest networks.
Ecuador.tip: Ecuador uses the US dollar — no exchange needed, just bring/withdraw USD and keep small bills ($20s and under; change is scarce). On the coast (Montañita) ATMs are limited and run dry — stock cash in Guayaquil first.

Peru.fee: Most ATMs charge ~$4–6; BCP, Interbank and Scotiabank are reliable and dispense soles or USD.
Peru.lim: BCP/Interbank often allow up to 700–1,000 PEN; some cap lower.
Peru.tip: Withdraw soles and DECLINE conversion. Use ATMs inside banks/malls, especially in Cusco's tourist centre. Globalnet standalone machines charge more — prefer the bank-branded ones. Carry small notes for markets and menús.

Chile.fee: Chilean ATMs are notorious for high foreign-card fees ($6–8) and often ask an intimidating 'foreign card' surcharge screen.
Chile.lim: Often capped at 200,000 CLP per pull (some banks more).
Chile.tip: Withdraw the maximum to dilute the flat fee, and choose pesos while declining conversion. Some travellers find Scotiabank and BancoEstado kinder. Chile is card-friendly, so you need less cash than you'd think.

Bolivia.fee: ATMs charge modest fees but can be finicky with foreign cards — carry a backup card.
Bolivia.lim: Often capped around 1,500–2,000 BOB per pull.
Bolivia.tip: Try a few banks if one rejects your card (common). Withdraw bolivianos, decline conversion, and keep small notes — change is scarce. Use ATMs in daylight inside branches; La Paz has plenty in Sopocachi and the centre.

Argentina.fee: AVOID ATMs here: they charge brutal fees ($10+), cap withdrawals painfully low, and give the poor official rate.
Argentina.lim: Often just 15,000–40,000 ARS per pull — dreadful value with the fee.
Argentina.tip: Argentina is the big exception: bring clean USD cash and change it at the favourable 'blue'/MEP-linked rate (via Western Union payout or trusted cambios), which can nearly DOUBLE your money versus ATMs. Many cards now also bill at the better MEP rate — check yours. Cash is king; plan ahead.

Brazil.fee: Use Banco24Horas, Bradesco, Santander or Banco do Brasil; many other machines block foreign cards or charge heavily. ~$5–6 typical.
Brazil.lim: Often capped around R$1,000–1,500 (lower at night for security).
Brazil.tip: Withdraw by day inside banks/malls (night limits drop for safety), choose reais, decline conversion. Brazil is very card/Pix-friendly, so carry only modest cash — 'beach money' for the sand, card for the rest.

China.fee: Foreign cards work at Bank of China, ICBC and big-bank ATMs (~¥15–30 fee), but China is almost entirely cashless via mobile pay.
China.tip: Set up Alipay or WeChat Pay with a foreign card BEFORE you go — you'll pay for nearly everything by QR, and cash is increasingly refused. Keep a little cash as backup and withdraw at major bank branches. Decline conversion.

Japan.fee: Use 7-Eleven (7-Bank) and Japan Post Bank ATMs — they reliably accept foreign cards with low/no surcharge. Many other ATMs reject foreign cards.
Japan.tip: Japan is still surprisingly cash-based for a rich country — carry more yen than you'd expect. 7-Eleven ATMs are your reliable friend, open 24/7 in every konbini. Decline conversion; pay in yen.

South Korea.fee: Look for 'Global ATM' signs (at convenience stores, banks); those take foreign cards for ~₩3,500. Many domestic-only ATMs won't.
South Korea.tip: A transit card (T-money) and a card cover most of life. Use 'Global ATM'-marked machines for cash, decline conversion, and keep some won for markets and older eateries.

Cambodia.fee: ATMs charge a flat $4–6 and, usefully, dispense US dollars (the de facto currency).
Cambodia.lim: Often $500 per pull; some allow more.
Cambodia.tip: Cambodia runs on US dollars — bring/withdraw clean USD and you'll rarely need riel (used only for small change). ABA has the best app and machines. Keep small, unmarked bills; torn notes get refused.

Laos.fee: ATMs charge ~20,000–30,000 kip per withdrawal with low limits.
Laos.lim: Often just 1–2 M kip per pull — withdraw the max to dilute the fee.
Laos.tip: Bring some USD or Thai baht as backup (widely accepted for larger bills). BCEL has the widest ATM network. Kip for everyday spends; decline conversion. Cash is king in laid-back Laos.

Sri Lanka.fee: ATMs charge ~₨400–600 per withdrawal; Commercial Bank and Sampath are reliable for foreign cards.
Sri Lanka.tip: Withdraw rupees at bank ATMs in towns (Ella's are limited — stock up in Kandy/Colombo). Use the PickMe app for fair tuk-tuk fares. Decline conversion; keep small notes.

Nepal.fee: ATMs charge a flat ~₨500 (Nepali) per withdrawal with lowish limits.
Nepal.tip: Withdraw the maximum to dilute the flat fee. Pokhara's Lakeside has plenty of ATMs. Carry cash for trekking (no ATMs on the trails) and small notes for tea houses. Decline conversion.

Australia.fee: Big-four bank ATMs (CommBank, Westpac, NAB, ANZ) are surcharge-free for withdrawals; standalone machines in pubs/shops charge $2–3.
Australia.tip: Australia is heavily card/tap — you'll barely need cash. Use big-four bank ATMs to avoid fees, tap for everything else, and always decline the currency conversion.

New Zealand.fee: Bank ATMs (ANZ, ASB, BNZ, Westpac) are surcharge-free for withdrawals.
New Zealand.tip: NZ is almost entirely card/PayWave — cash is rarely needed. Draw from bank ATMs if you want some, tap for the rest, and decline conversion (pay in NZ dollars).

Thailand.vax: Routine shots up to date, plus Hepatitis A and (for street-food adventurers) Typhoid. Rabies and Japanese encephalitis only for long rural stays — a travel clinic will tell you in five minutes.
Thailand.health: Dengue mosquitoes bite at dawn and dusk — repellent is the one habit that matters. Skip tap water (sealed bottles and purified ice are everywhere); busy stalls with turnover are the safe street food. Private hospitals are world-class and affordable — Bangkok is where the region flies for treatment.
Thailand.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Sealed bottled water is cheap and everywhere; ice in established places is factory-made and fine.
Thailand.safe: Violent crime against visitors is genuinely rare — the real risk wears two wheels: traffic. Helmet on every scooter, Grab at night, and you've handled 90 % of it. Classic scams (gem shops, 'closed temple' tuk-tuks) are annoyances, not dangers — a smile and a walk-on solves them.

Malaysia.vax: Routine plus Hepatitis A; Typhoid if you'll eat adventurously (you should).
Malaysia.health: Dengue is present — repellent at dusk. Most locals drink filtered water; do the same. Private healthcare (KL, Penang) is excellent and inexpensive; pharmacies dispense competently everywhere.
Malaysia.water: ⚠️ Officially treated but most locals boil or filter it — stick to bottled or filtered to be safe.
Malaysia.safe: One of Southeast Asia's calmest countries. The single habit to build: carry bags on the building side of the pavement — motorbike snatch theft is the local specialty, easily beaten. East-coast islands close in the Nov–Feb monsoon; the west coast (Penang!) shines year-round as your alternative.

Vietnam.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Rabies awareness around street dogs — don't pet, and any bite means a clinic same-day.
Vietnam.health: Bottled water, cooked food, repellent for dengue — the classic tropical trio. International clinics (Vinmec, Family Medical) in Hanoi, Da Nang and Saigon are excellent.
Vietnam.water: ❌ Not safe to drink. Bottled only; refill stations exist in tourist towns to cut plastic.
Vietnam.safe: Extremely low violent crime. The famous hazard is crossing the street: walk out slowly, keep a steady pace, and the motorbike river flows around you — it genuinely works. Phone-snatching from motorbikes exists in Saigon: hold it away from the curb.

Indonesia.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Bali has rabies in dogs and monkeys — admire, don't touch; any scratch (looking at you, Monkey Forest) means a clinic that day.
Indonesia.health: 'Bali belly' is mostly avoidable: sealed water, hot cooked food, peeled fruit. One serious rule with a simple fix: drink only sealed, branded spirits — informal arak has caused methanol poisonings. On Gili Air, cuts from coral are the main 'injury' — pack reef shoes and antiseptic. BIMC and Siloam hospitals in Bali are solid.
Indonesia.water: ❌ Never drink the tap (Bali belly's main culprit). Sealed bottles only; on Gili Air, carry enough over.
Indonesia.safe: Homicide rates here are among the world's lowest — day-to-day Bali and the Gilis feel gentler than most European cities. Petty theft from parked scooters is the main nuisance: use the seat lock. Volcanoes occasionally grumble; if Agung is active, flights reroute and the authorities are well-drilled.

Philippines.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid; rabies awareness with strays.
Philippines.health: Bottled water, repellent for dengue, sunscreen like it's a job — the tropics' honest checklist. City private hospitals (Cebu Doctors', Chong Hua) are good; island clinics are basic, so travel insured.
Philippines.water: ⚠️ Metro Manila and Cebu tap is chlorinated but most drink bottled/purified; on islands, always bottled.
Philippines.safe: The tourist islands — Boracay, Bohol, Cebu's resorts — run calm and heavily hosted; violence involving visitors is rare there. National statistics look higher than your actual itinerary: the areas driving them (far southwest Mindanao) are 500+ km from anywhere on this site. Typhoon season is Jun–Nov; Dec–May is your blue-sky alternative.

North Macedonia.vax: Routine only. Hikers doing Pelister forests in spring–summer: ask about tick-borne encephalitis and wear long trousers on trails.
North Macedonia.health: Tap water in Skopje, Ohrid and Bitola is safe and good. Pharmacies are plentiful; EU-standard care is a short hop away.
North Macedonia.water: ✅ Safe and good — Skopje, Ohrid and Bitola tap water is clean mountain supply. Drink freely.
North Macedonia.safe: Homicide ~1 per 100k — safer than most of Western Europe's big cities. Ohrid in August is crowded, not dangerous; the only 'risk' worth planning around is Skopje's winter smog — visit May–October and it's moot.

Serbia.vax: Routine only; tick-borne encephalitis shot for serious forest hikers.
Serbia.health: Belgrade and Novi Sad tap water: drink it. Healthcare is competent; private clinics quick and cheap.
Serbia.water: ✅ Safe in Belgrade and Novi Sad — city tap water is fine to drink.
Serbia.safe: Belgrade at 3 am is famously relaxed — violent street crime toward visitors is rare (~1/100k homicide). The one date to plan around: derby football nights (Partizan–Red Star), when stadium districts get rowdy — the kafanas across town are your better evening anyway.

Montenegro.health: Tap water is fine on the coast. Summer sun is fierce on those white stone streets — hats and water. At Ada Bojana, swim the lagoon side with kids; where river meets sea the current is honest.
Montenegro.water: ✅ Coastal tap water is safe to drink; refill and skip the bottles.
Montenegro.safe: Coastal Montenegro is small-town safe (~2/100k). The genuine risk is the roads: twisty, dramatic, occasionally shared with confident drivers — take the bus at night and it's solved. August crowds are the other 'hazard'; June and September are the same sea, calmer.

Egypt.health: Bottled water only, and give your stomach two gentle days before the buffet victory lap. The Red Sea repays respect: reef shoes, no touching coral, and dive only with CDWS-listed shops. Sun is desert-serious — hydrate beyond thirst.
Egypt.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap, and skip loose ice outside good hotels. Bottled water only — check the seal.
Egypt.safe: Hurghada's resort coast is one of the most heavily protected tourist zones anywhere — petty crime is notably rare. The advisories you'll read concern North Sinai, a full country-width away from the Red Sea resorts. Haggling theatrics are the local sport; play or smile-decline, both work.

Mauritius.vax: Routine; dengue appears in occasional outbreaks — repellent in wet season (Nov–Apr).
Mauritius.health: Water is officially treated; most visitors drink bottled after cyclones stir the pipes. On rocky lagoon entries wear water shoes (stonefish are rare but real). Clinics are good; Apollo Bramwell-class private care exists.
Mauritius.water: ⚠️ Officially treated and generally safe, but many visitors prefer bottled after cyclones stir the supply.
Mauritius.safe: One of Africa's safest countries by every index — families wander night markets without a thought. Beach rule: don't leave bags unattended while you swim. Cyclone season peaks Jan–Feb; May–Dec is your serene alternative.

Czechia.vax: Routine. Forest hikers: Czechia is a tick-borne encephalitis hotspot — the vaccine is worth asking about for countryside trips; city breaks need nothing.
Czechia.health: Tap water excellent. Pharmacies (lékárna) are everywhere and capable.
Czechia.water: ✅ Excellent — Prague tap water is high quality. Bring a refillable bottle.
Czechia.safe: Prague's violent-crime rate is among Europe's lowest (~0.7/100k). The entire risk profile is pickpockets on Old Town Square, Charles Bridge and tram 22 — front pockets, zipped bags, done. That, and the exchange kiosks we've already banned you from.

Slovakia.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for Tatra hikers.
Slovakia.water: ✅ Excellent and safe straight from the tap.
Slovakia.safe: Bratislava is a small, calm capital — the statistics barely register. Weekend stag groups are louder than any local danger; two streets away is silence.

Romania.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for Carpathian hikes.
Romania.health: City tap water is treated (many prefer bottled for taste). Stray dogs in outskirts: don't engage, carry on. Private clinics (Regina Maria, MedLife) are quick and inexpensive.
Romania.water: ✅ City tap water is treated and safe; many prefer bottled purely for taste.
Romania.safe: Bucharest is statistically safer than Paris or Brussels for violent crime. Old-town clip joints and 'meter' taxis are the actual traps — both die instantly to apps and our restaurant rules. Peleș and the mountains: standard hiking sense.

Poland.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis if you'll do eastern forests.
Poland.water: ✅ Safe to drink across the country; Gdańsk tap is good.
Poland.safe: Gdańsk and the Tricity are Baltic-calm (~0.7/100k nationally). Summer weekend party crowds in Sopot are boisterous, not threatening. The Baltic itself is the thing to respect: swim at flagged beaches; that sea is colder and stronger than it looks.

Estonia.vax: Routine; the Baltics have real tick-borne encephalitis — vaccine worthwhile if bog-walks and forests are on your list.
Estonia.health: Tap water excellent; e-health so advanced your prescription is a QR code.
Estonia.water: ✅ Excellent, safe, and among Europe's cleanest — drink from the tap.
Estonia.safe: Tallinn ranks among the EU's safest capitals. Winter's real hazard is horizontal: icy pavements — pack grippy soles, walk like a penguin, and you've mastered Estonian winter safety.

Latvia.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for forest and Jūrmala-dune wanderers.
Latvia.water: ✅ Safe to drink; Riga's supply is fine straight from the tap.
Latvia.safe: Rīga's old town is peaceful; the historical 'gentlemen's bar' bill-trap is the one local scam — stick to listed venues (our rule already). Winter ice, same penguin protocol as Tallinn.

Italy.health: Tap water is excellent — Milan's is alpine. Pharmacies (farmacia) handle minor everything. August heat in Florence is real: museums at noon, piazzas at dusk.
Italy.water: ✅ Excellent everywhere — Rome's 'nasoni' street fountains are free, safe and delicious. Refill constantly.
Italy.safe: Violent crime toward visitors: statistically tiny. Pickpocketing near Milano Centrale, the Duomo and Florence's buses is professional-grade — money in front pockets, backpacks worn forward on transit, and you're invisible to them. That's the whole briefing.

France.health: Tap water fine (ask for 'une carafe d'eau' — it's free). Pharmacies are French national treasures.
France.water: ✅ Safe nationwide — ask for 'une carafe d'eau' free at any restaurant.
France.safe: Paris is far safer than its reputation among people who watch too much news (~1.2/100k). Métro lines 1 and 4 and the Sacré-Cœur steps host Europe's most artistic pickpockets — phone in pocket before the doors open. The gold-ring and petition performers are street theatre; keep walking, enjoy the show.

Belgium.water: ✅ Safe to drink from the tap everywhere.
Belgium.safe: Brussels' tourist core is calm; Gare du Midi arrivals is the one pickpocket hotspot — bag zipped, then waffles. Late-night around the station district: take a cab like a local would.

United Kingdom.health: Tap water great; pharmacies and NHS walk-in centres handle traveller mishaps. Edinburgh weather is the health hazard: four seasons before lunch — layer.
United Kingdom.water: ✅ Excellent and safe — Edinburgh tap water is soft and clean. Refill freely.
United Kingdom.safe: Edinburgh is one of the UK's safest cities. Weekend Cowgate gets merry rather than menacing; licensed cabs home and it's a non-topic. Arthur's Seat in proper shoes, not after the third whisky.

Portugal.health: Tap water fine. The Atlantic is the one force to respect: swim at flagged beaches — those currents are honest even in July.
Portugal.water: ✅ Safe to drink; coastal areas can taste faintly of chlorine but it's fine.
Portugal.safe: Portugal sits in the global top-10 of the Peace Index — one of the safest countries you can visit, full stop. Tram 28 pickpockets and the friendly 'hash?' oregano salesmen of Lisbon are the entire threat landscape. Both are beaten by a zipped bag and a smile.

Spain.health: Tap water fine everywhere on our list (coastal areas vary in taste, not safety). July–August heat inland (Sevilla, Madrid!) is genuinely fierce — siesta culture exists for a reason; May–June and Sept–Oct are golden alternatives.
Spain.water: ✅ Safe nationwide (Madrid's is famously good); some coastal spots taste briny but remain safe.
Spain.safe: Violent crime toward visitors: among Europe's lowest. Barcelona is, however, the continent's pickpocket capital — Las Ramblas, metro L3, and beach bags are the arenas. Phone gripped, bag worn forward, nothing valuable on the sand: play that defense and Spain is pure joy.

Norway.health: Tap water is some of the world's best. Real risks live outdoors: weather turns fast on hikes (check yr.no religiously, tell someone your route), and fjord water is arrestingly cold year-round.
Norway.water: ✅ Among the world's best — drink straight from any tap with pride.
Norway.safe: Statistically among the safest countries on Earth. Oslo's east-side nightlife districts are lively, not dangerous. Your genuine adversaries: hiking weather and the bar tab.

Sweden.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis if you'll do southern-coast forests or the archipelago in summer.
Sweden.health: Tap water superb; healthcare excellent (bring your EHIC/GHIC if European).
Sweden.water: ✅ Superb, safe, and free everywhere — no need to ever buy bottled.
Sweden.safe: The gang-related incidents in Swedish headlines happen in outer suburbs with no tourist presence whatsoever — central Stockholm, Gothenburg and Malmö rank with Europe's calmest city centres for visitors. Winter ice and summer boat-beers-swimming combos deserve more caution than any street.

Finland.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for Åland/coastal summer wanderers.
Finland.health: Tap water is a national pride; pharmacies (apteekki) excellent.
Finland.water: ✅ A national pride — some of the cleanest tap water on Earth. Refill anywhere.
Finland.safe: Finland is routinely ranked the world's happiest and among its safest — Helsinki's biggest danger is buying more Marimekko than your luggage allows. Winter: ice grips for shoes, and never walk on sea ice without locals doing it first.

United States.health: Tap water fine. The health story here is financial: US care is superb and staggeringly expensive — travel insurance isn't optional, it's the trip's most important booking. Sun and rip currents: swim near lifeguard flags, always.
United States.water: ✅ Tap water is safe and free — ask for it at any restaurant. Refill stations are common.
United States.safe: Miami's beaches and tourist districts are heavily patrolled and busy till late. American city safety is block-by-block: stay where the people are, rideshare after midnight rather than wandering, and it's a normal big-city visit. Hurricane season Jun–Nov; Dec–Apr is the postcard window.

Dominican Republic.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid; repellent for dengue.
Dominican Republic.health: Bottled water; resort food is fine, street food from busy spots. Pack rehydration salts — the sun does the rest of the talking.
Dominican Republic.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled water only, even at many resorts (they'll provide it).
Dominican Republic.safe: The Punta Cana resort corridor has its own tourist police force (CESTUR) and runs very calm. Book excursions with licensed operators, skip moto-taxis after dark, keep resort-safe habits with valuables — standard Caribbean sense. Hurricane peak Aug–Oct; Dec–Apr is prime.

Netherlands.health: Tap water excellent. The genuine hazard is the bike lane — look both ways twice, never walk in the red-paved lanes.
Netherlands.water: ✅ Excellent and strictly regulated — drink freely from any tap.
Netherlands.safe: Amsterdam is very safe (~1/100k). Pickpockets work Centraal and the crush around the Red Light District; bikes will run you over before any criminal will. The 'coffeeshop' rules are legal but city-specific — read the signs.

Austria.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for alpine hikers.
Austria.health: Tap water is alpine-pure. Vienna's healthcare is world-class.
Austria.water: ✅ Alpine-pure — Vienna's tap water flows straight from the mountains. Superb.
Austria.safe: Vienna is routinely named among the world's safest and most liveable cities. The whole risk profile is transit pickpockets around Stephansplatz — zip your bag and relax.

Hungary.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for forest hikers.
Hungary.health: Budapest tap water is excellent; the thermal baths are a health feature, not a hazard (shower first, hydrate after).
Hungary.water: ✅ Budapest tap water is safe and good; refill your bottle.
Hungary.safe: Budapest is a safe capital (~1/100k). The real traps are financial: rigged taxis (use Bolt), inflated 'ruin bar' tabs, and the old exchange-kiosk scam — all beaten by our standing rules.

Greece.vax: Routine, plus Hepatitis A for wider eating.
Greece.health: Tap water is safe in Athens; on many islands it's brackish — locals drink bottled, so do the same. Summer sun and meltemi wind are fierce; hydrate and respect ferry cancellations.
Greece.water: ⚠️ Safe in Athens and the mainland; on many islands it's brackish or unreliable, so locals drink bottled — do the same there.
Greece.safe: Greece is very safe for visitors (~1/100k). Athens' Omonia and Exarcheia get edgier at night; the islands are family-gentle. Watch bags on the crowded metro to the Acropolis.

Croatia.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for continental forest hikes.
Croatia.health: Tap water is excellent countrywide. On rocky Adriatic entries wear water shoes (sea urchins). Sun is strong on the white stone.
Croatia.water: ✅ Excellent countrywide, including Dubrovnik and Split — drink from the tap.
Croatia.safe: One of Europe's safest countries — Dubrovnik and Split feel effortlessly calm. Old-town crowds in summer are the only 'crush'. Swim shoes and shade are the real advisories.

Germany.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for southern forests.
Germany.water: ✅ Safe and high quality everywhere (Leitungswasser); Berlin's is fine to drink.
Germany.safe: Berlin is safe and famously easygoing (~1/100k). Pickpockets favour Alexanderplatz, Warschauer and the U-Bahn; that's the extent of it. Look left for cyclists before you step off any kerb.

Ireland.health: Tap water fine; Dublin's weather is the health story — layer, it rains sideways.
Ireland.water: ✅ Safe to drink nationwide; Dublin tap water is fine.
Ireland.safe: Dublin is friendly and broadly safe; late-night around parts of the north inner city and the boardwalk can feel edgy — stick to busy streets and taxi home. Pickpockets work Grafton Street crowds.

Denmark.water: ✅ Excellent — Copenhagen tap water is clean and safe. Skip bottled.
Denmark.safe: Copenhagen is one of the world's safest capitals — kids cycle everywhere. The only real rule is bike-lane awareness. Christiania has its own etiquette: no photos on Pusher Street.

Iceland.health: Tap water is glacial and perfect (skip bottled entirely). The hazards are natural: sudden weather, unfenced cliffs, geothermal-hot ground, and rip currents at Reynisfjara's black beach — heed every sign.
Iceland.water: ✅ Some of the purest on Earth — glacial and free. Never buy bottled here; it's a tourist trap.
Iceland.safe: Iceland is statistically the safest country on Earth (near-zero violent crime). Your only genuine adversaries are the weather and your own selfie confidence near cliffs and waves. Check road.is and safetravel.is.

Switzerland.vax: Routine; tick-borne encephalitis for alpine hikers.
Switzerland.health: Tap water is drinkable everywhere, even most mountain fountains. Care is superb and famously expensive — insure well. Altitude on peak excursions is real.
Switzerland.water: ✅ Superb and drinkable everywhere, including most labelled mountain fountains. Refill constantly.
Switzerland.safe: Switzerland is among the safest countries anywhere. Zürich's nightlife district (Langstrasse) is the one livelier corner. Mountain weather and expensive mistakes are the actual risks.

Mexico.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Rabies awareness for long rural stays.
Mexico.health: Stick to bottled/purified water; the 'agua purificada' garrafón is everywhere. Street food from busy stalls with turnover is the safe kind. Altitude in Mexico City (2,240m) can wind you the first day. Private hospitals in cities are excellent and affordable.
Mexico.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled/purified 'agua purificada' is universal and cheap; good restaurants use it for ice too.
Mexico.safe: Your itinerary matters more than the national headlines. Tourist Yucatán (Mérida is among Mexico's safest cities), Oaxaca and CDMX's central neighbourhoods run calm and busy. Use Uber/Didi over street cabs, ATMs inside banks/malls, and skip flashy valuables. The cartel-linked violence that drives statistics is concentrated in specific states far from these places.

Cuba.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A; Typhoid for wider eating. Bring any prescription meds you need — pharmacies are sparsely stocked.
Cuba.health: Drink bottled water only. Carry your own basics (painkillers, rehydration salts, sunscreen) — shortages are real and shops may simply not have them. Tourist clinics (Cira García in Havana) serve foreigners for cash.
Cuba.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled water can itself be scarce — buy it when you see it and keep a reserve.
Cuba.safe: One of Latin America's safest countries for visitors — violent crime is rare and tourists are generally left in peace. The real challenges are practical: cash-only economy, shortages of food/fuel/medicine, and long queues. Petty scams (rigged taxis, 'closed' restaurants steering you elsewhere) are the main annoyance.

Guatemala.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Rabies awareness rurally; malaria pills only for low-lying jungle stays (not Antigua/Atitlán highlands).
Guatemala.health: Bottled/purified water only. Antigua and Atitlán sit at altitude (1,500m+), so cooler and gentler on the stomach. Volcano hikes need real shoes and a guide. Antigua has decent private clinics; serious cases go to Guatemala City.
Guatemala.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Purified 'agua pura' is cheap and everywhere.
Guatemala.safe: Antigua and Lake Atitlán are the well-trodden traveller circuit and feel relaxed and hosted; Guatemala City is best transited quickly. Use tourist shuttles or Uber in the capital, don't hike volcanoes solo, and keep valuables low-key. Chicken buses are colourful but pickpocket-prone.

Nicaragua.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Dengue present — repellent; malaria pills only for remote lowlands.
Nicaragua.health: Bottled/purified water. León is hot and low — hydrate hard and sunscreen up. Volcano boarding is a blast but wear the gear. Private clinics in León and Managua handle basics; travel insured for anything serious.
Nicaragua.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Purified water is cheap and easy to find.
Nicaragua.safe: Historically one of the region's safest for travellers, with low violent crime. Note the political situation can bring occasional demonstrations — avoid protests and check current advisories before you go. Otherwise standard petty-theft sense covers it.

Costa Rica.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A; Typhoid for wider eating. Dengue on both coasts — repellent.
Costa Rica.health: Tap water is actually safe to drink in most of the country including San José — a Central American rarity. Rip currents on both coasts are the real hazard: swim at flagged beaches, respect the ocean. Excellent private hospitals (CIMA, Clínica Bíblica).
Costa Rica.water: ✅ Safe to drink in most of the country, including cities and most beach towns — a regional exception. In very remote spots, ask locally.
Costa Rica.safe: One of Latin America's safest and most visitor-ready countries ('pura vida' is real). Petty theft from cars and beaches is the main issue — never leave anything visible in a rental, use lockers. Santa Teresa and Puerto Viejo are laid-back surf towns; standard beach-town smarts apply.

Panama.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A; Typhoid for wider eating. Dengue present; yellow-fever shot only if heading to Darién (not Bocas or the city).
Panama.health: Panama City tap water is safe to drink; on Bocas del Toro islands drink bottled. Caribbean sun and reef cuts are the Bocas hazards — reef shoes, sunscreen. Panama City has first-rate private hospitals (Punta Pacífica).
Panama.water: ⚠️ Safe in Panama City; on Bocas del Toro and remote islands, drink bottled.
Panama.safe: Panama City and Bocas del Toro are calm and tourist-friendly. Standard city sense in the capital (Uber, ATMs indoors); Bocas is a mellow island-hopper's town. Avoid the Darién Gap entirely — it's a genuine no-go, nowhere near your route.

Colombia.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Yellow-fever shot recommended for Cartagena/coast and required for some parks — get it 10 days ahead.
Colombia.health: Bottled/purified water (Medellín's tap is actually potable and good). Cartagena's Caribbean heat is intense — hydrate and pace. Excellent, affordable private healthcare, especially in Medellín (a medical-tourism hub).
Colombia.water: ⚠️ Medellín and Bogotá tap water is safe and good; on the Caribbean coast (Cartagena) stick to bottled.
Colombia.safe: 'No dar papaya' is the local rule — don't flash anything worth stealing and you remove most risk. Medellín's El Poblado/Laureles and Cartagena's walled city and Getsemaní are geared for visitors and feel relaxed by day. Use Uber/inDrive, ATMs indoors, and don't wander empty streets late. Scopolamine ('devil's breath') scams are real — never accept drinks or cigarettes from strangers.

Venezuela.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Yellow-fever shot recommended; malaria pills for some regions. Bring all your own medicines — pharmacies are severely under-stocked.
Venezuela.health: Bottled water only, and carry a full personal medical kit; the healthcare system is in crisis and shortages of medicines are severe. Serious issues mean private clinics (cash/USD) or medical evacuation — insure specifically for Venezuela.
Venezuela.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled water is essential and worth stocking up when available.
Venezuela.safe: Be honest with yourself here: Caracas has among the world's highest crime rates, and most governments advise heightened caution or reconsidering non-essential travel. If you go, go with local contacts or a trusted guide, don't walk with a phone out, avoid the city after dark, use only arranged transport (not street taxis), and keep a very low profile. Check your government's advisory carefully before booking — this is the one destination on Sama·Sama where that step isn't optional.

Ecuador.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Yellow-fever shot for Amazon regions (not coastal Montañita). Malaria pills only for jungle lowlands.
Ecuador.health: Bottled/purified water. Coastal Montañita is hot and sunny — hydrate, sunscreen, and respect the surf. Altitude matters if you combine with Quito (2,850m). Guayaquil has the nearest good hospitals to the coast.
Ecuador.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Purified water is cheap and everywhere.
Ecuador.safe: Ecuador has seen rising crime in some cities (notably Guayaquil), so check current advisories. Montañita itself is a small, laid-back surf-party town — the usual beach-town sense covers it: watch valuables, don't walk the beach alone very late, moderate the party. Use registered taxis or Uber/inDrive.

Peru.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Yellow-fever shot for Amazon (not Cusco/coast). Rabies awareness for long rural stays.
Peru.health: Bottled/purified water only. Cusco sits at 3,400m — altitude sickness is real: arrive slow, hydrate, coca tea helps, consider acetazolamide. Máncora on the coast is hot and low. Cusco has clinics used to altitude cases; Lima has top hospitals.
Peru.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Purified water is cheap; at altitude, hydration matters even more.
Peru.safe: The Gringo Trail (Cusco, Sacred Valley, Máncora) is well-worn and generally safe. Cusco is very tourist-geared; watch bags in crowds and use registered taxis or Uber. Máncora is a mellow surf town with standard beach-town smarts. Don't hike remote trails solo without a guide.

Chile.vax: Routine; Hepatitis A for wider eating. One of the region's lowest health-risk countries.
Chile.health: Tap water is safe to drink in Valparaíso and Santiago (it can be very mineral-heavy, so some prefer bottled for taste). Excellent healthcare. Strong Pacific sun and cool ocean — the Humboldt current makes beaches chilly.
Chile.water: ✅ Safe to drink in Valparaíso and central Chile (high mineral content — some prefer bottled for taste, not safety).
Chile.safe: Chile is among South America's safest and most developed countries. Valparaíso is characterful but has rougher hillside pockets — stay on the tourist cerros (Alegre, Concepción), watch your phone in crowds, and take registered taxis/Uber at night. Petty theft is the main concern, not violence.

Bolivia.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Yellow-fever shot for lowland/Amazon regions. Rabies awareness rurally.
Bolivia.health: Bottled/purified water only. La Paz is extreme altitude (3,600m, El Alto higher) — take the first day very slow, hydrate, mate de coca helps a lot. Clinics in La Paz handle altitude routinely; serious cases may need descent or evacuation.
Bolivia.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Purified water is cheap; altitude makes hydration essential.
Bolivia.safe: Bolivia is relatively safe for travellers with mostly petty crime. In La Paz use radio taxis or apps (not random street cabs — 'express kidnapping' scams exist), keep bags close in markets, and beware fake-police scams (real police never demand to see your money or search you in the street). Protests can block roads — build in flexibility.

Argentina.vax: Routine; Hepatitis A for wider eating. Low health risk overall.
Argentina.health: Buenos Aires tap water is safe to drink. Excellent private healthcare. The main 'health' event is eating steak and drinking Malbec at 10pm like a local — pace yourself.
Argentina.water: ✅ Safe to drink in Buenos Aires and major cities.
Argentina.safe: Buenos Aires is a big, late-night European-feeling city — generally safe in the tourist barrios (Palermo, Recoleta, San Telmo, Puerto Madero) but with real petty theft and phone-snatching. Keep your phone off the table on the street, use Uber/Cabify, and change money smartly (see the cash tab — the 'blue' rate matters here). La Boca only by day, main streets only.

Brazil.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Yellow-fever shot is recommended for much of Brazil incl. Rio state — get it 10 days before travel. Dengue present; repellent.
Brazil.health: Bottled/filtered water. Tropical sun on Rio and Floripa beaches is fierce — sunscreen and hydration. Excellent private hospitals in big cities. Watch the surf: strong currents on Atlantic beaches, swim between the flags.
Brazil.water: ⚠️ Big-city tap is treated but most drink filtered/bottled; on the coast and islands, bottled.
Brazil.safe: Rio rewards street-smarts: enjoy the famous beaches and sights by day, keep phones and jewellery out of sight, carry only what you need ('beach money'), and use Uber/99 rather than walking unfamiliar areas at night. Favelas only with a reputable guide. Florianópolis is markedly calmer — a laid-back island of beaches. Standard big-city and beach-town sense covers both.

China.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Japanese encephalitis for long rural/summer stays.
China.health: Bottled/boiled water only. Air quality varies by city and season — check the AQI, sensitive travellers pack a mask. Big-city international hospitals are excellent (and pricey); insure well.
China.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled or boiled water only; hotels provide kettles and locals drink hot water everywhere.
China.safe: China is very safe for visitors day-to-day — violent crime against tourists is rare and cities feel secure late at night. The real friction is digital: bring a VPN installed BEFORE arrival (Google, WhatsApp, Instagram are blocked), and set up Alipay/WeChat Pay with a foreign card — cash is nearly dead here. Scams target tourists at tea houses and 'art galleries' near sights.

Japan.vax: Routine only — Japan is very low health-risk.
Japan.health: Tap water is excellent and safe everywhere. Pharmacies are ubiquitous; summers are hot and humid (hydrate), and the odd typhoon hits Jul–Oct. Healthcare is superb; carry your insurance details.
Japan.water: ✅ Excellent and safe to drink from any tap nationwide.
Japan.safe: Japan is among the safest countries on Earth — lost wallets get returned, women travel solo comfortably, crime is remarkably low. The genuine risks are natural: earthquakes (know the drill) and typhoons. Learn a little train etiquette and you'll glide.

South Korea.vax: Routine only; Hepatitis A for wider street-food eating.
South Korea.health: Tap water is safe (though many locals prefer bottled/filtered by taste). Excellent, affordable healthcare. Hot humid summers; fine dust (미세먼지) days in spring — check the AQI and mask up if sensitive.
South Korea.water: ✅ Safe to drink from the tap; locals often prefer bottled for taste, not safety.
South Korea.safe: South Korea is extremely safe with very low crime — Seoul and Busan feel secure around the clock. The main things to watch: heavy nightlife districts on weekends and spring dust days. Superb, cheap public transport everywhere.

Cambodia.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Japanese encephalitis and malaria pills for rural/jungle stays (not Siem Reap town). Rabies awareness.
Cambodia.health: Bottled water only. Fierce sun at Angkor — start at dawn, hydrate, cover up. Dengue present, use repellent. Siem Reap has decent clinics (Royal Angkor); serious cases go to Bangkok.
Cambodia.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled water is cheap and everywhere; check the seal.
Cambodia.safe: Siem Reap is a well-trodden, welcoming tourist town and generally very safe. Watch for bag-snatching from motorbikes (wear bags cross-body, away from the road), and only use reputable tuk-tuks/PassApp. Petty scams around temples are mild. Never touch unexploded-ordnance warning areas off the beaten path.

Laos.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Japanese encephalitis and malaria pills for rural stays. Rabies awareness.
Laos.health: Bottled water only. Luang Prabang is laid-back and low-altitude; the sun and river activities are the main hazards — sunscreen, life jackets on boats. Clinics are basic; anything serious means evacuation to Thailand, so insure well.
Laos.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled water only; it's cheap and widely sold.
Laos.safe: Laos is one of Southeast Asia's calmest, safest countries — Luang Prabang especially so, with a gentle curfew keeping nights quiet. Petty theft is the main (low) risk. Stick to marked paths in rural areas (historic UXO risk) and use licensed transport.

Sri Lanka.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Japanese encephalitis for long rural stays; dengue is present — repellent.
Sri Lanka.health: Bottled/filtered water. Ella is hill-country (cooler, gentler); the sun is still strong at altitude. Watch footing on the famous railway walks. Good private hospitals in Colombo/Kandy; Ella has basic clinics.
Sri Lanka.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled or filtered water; it's cheap and everywhere.
Sri Lanka.safe: Sri Lanka is warm and largely very safe for travellers, with low violent crime. Solo women should take standard care with unwanted attention. Tuk-tuk overcharging is the main hustle — use the PickMe app for metered fares. Watch your footing on the scenic (active) railway tracks around Ella.

Nepal.vax: Routine, Hepatitis A, Typhoid. Rabies awareness; Japanese encephalitis for the lowland Terai. Consider altitude meds if trekking high.
Nepal.health: Bottled/filtered/boiled water only. Pokhara sits at a comfortable 800m, but if you trek from here, altitude sickness is the serious risk — ascend slowly, know the symptoms. Kathmandu air is dusty. Clinics in Pokhara handle basics; serious cases go to Kathmandu.
Nepal.water: ❌ Don't drink the tap. Bottled, filtered or boiled only; refill stations reduce plastic.
Nepal.safe: Nepal is welcoming and generally safe, with mostly petty crime. In Pokhara the risks are outdoor: trekking without proper acclimatisation, lake/paragliding safety (use reputable operators), and monsoon landslides (Jun–Sep). Use registered trekking guides and check weather.

Australia.vax: Routine only — Australia is very low health-risk.
Australia.health: Tap water is excellent everywhere. The hazards are famously outdoors: ferocious sun (the world's highest skin-cancer rates — 'slip, slop, slap' sunscreen), rip currents (swim between the red-and-yellow flags), and respect for wildlife/heat on hikes. Superb healthcare; insure as it's costly for visitors.
Australia.water: ✅ Excellent and safe to drink from any tap nationwide.
Australia.safe: Australia is very safe with low violent crime. The real risks are natural: sun, surf rips (always swim between the flags), bushfire season (check warnings in summer), and heat on outback drives. City nightlife precincts get rowdy late weekend but rarely dangerous.

New Zealand.health: Tap water is pristine and safe. The intense hazard is UV — the ozone-thin sky burns fast, so sunscreen hard. Alpine and coastal weather turns quickly; respect track and marine safety. Excellent healthcare.
New Zealand.water: ✅ Pristine and safe to drink from any tap (in the backcountry, treat river water).
New Zealand.safe: New Zealand is among the world's safest countries with very low crime. The genuine risks are all outdoors: fierce UV, fast-changing alpine weather, cold water, and adventure activities (use licensed operators). Don't leave valuables visible in parked cars at trailheads — that's the one common theft.

Thailand.v: Easy if you say it right: 'jay' (เจ) means fully plant-based and every market has a jay stall. Watch fish sauce and oyster sauce — ask 'mai sai nam pla'.
Thailand.g: Rice-based heaven: most noodles and rice dishes are naturally gluten-free; soy sauce (wheat) hides in stir-fries — ask for 'no soy sauce'.
Thailand.t: Veg = 'gin jay' · no fish sauce = 'mai sai nam pla' · Bangkok's Chinatown runs a whole Jay festival every October.

Malaysia.v: Indian-Malaysian canteens are a vegetarian goldmine — banana-leaf thali, chapati, dhal for $2. 'Sayur saja' = vegetables only.
Malaysia.g: Rice and rice-noodle dishes dominate; watch soy and kicap in stir-fries, and roti/mee are wheat.
Malaysia.t: Look for 'vegetarian' mamak counters; Buddhist 'zhai' shops in George Town are fully plant-based.

Vietnam.v: 'Chay' means vegetarian and it's a whole cuisine — every town has quán chay eateries; phở chay, bánh mì chay all exist.
Vietnam.g: Phở and most noodle soups use rice noodles — naturally GF; soy sauce and seitan mock-meats are the traps.
Vietnam.t: Say 'ăn chay' (I eat veg) · fish sauce = nước mắm, ask to skip · the 1st & 15th lunar days, chay food is everywhere.

Indonesia.v: Tempeh and tofu are national treasures — gado-gado, urap, nasi campur can all go plant-based. Warung 'vegetarian' signs are common in Bali.
Indonesia.g: Rice-centred and largely GF by default; kecap manis (sweet soy) contains wheat — ask for plain sambal instead.
Indonesia.t: 'Tanpa terasi' skips the shrimp paste · Ubud is one of Asia's vegan capitals — entire raw/vegan menus.

Philippines.v: Hardest of the region — meat hides everywhere. Stick to Chinese-Filipino veggie houses, Bohol's farm cafés, and market fruit.
Philippines.g: Rice-based mains are safe; soy sauce (toyo) is in most adobo and marinades — grilled fish + rice is the reliable order.
Philippines.t: 'Walang karne' = no meat · 'gulay lang' = just vegetables · big cities have growing vegan scenes (Cebu IT Park).

North Macedonia.v: Fast-day (posna) food is your friend — Orthodox fasting dishes are vegan by rule: tavče gravče, ajvar, grilled peppers, beans.
North Macedonia.g: Grills (skara) are naturally GF; burek and bread are the wheat walls. Say 'bez gluten'.
North Macedonia.t: 'Posno' on a menu = plant-based by religious definition — the oldest vegan hack in the Balkans.

Serbia.v: Same posna trick: fasting menus (prebranac beans, sarma without meat, grilled veg) are everywhere, especially Wednesdays/Fridays.
Serbia.g: Meat off the grill is GF; burek, lepinja bread and beer are not. GF shops exist in Belgrade's malls.
Serbia.t: 'Posna hrana' = fasting food = vegan · kajmak and cheeses rule the veg-etarian (not vegan) table.

Montenegro.v: Coastal menus lean fish + grilled veg; posna dishes and excellent tomatoes-cheese-olive spreads carry vegetarians.
Montenegro.g: Grilled fish and meats are safe; bread arrives with everything — just wave it off.
Montenegro.t: 'Bez mesa' = without meat · konoba owners will improvise happily if you ask.

Egypt.v: Accidentally vegan national dishes: koshary, ful medames, ta'ameya (fava falafel) — the cheapest food is the plant-based food.
Egypt.g: Koshary is pasta-based (wheat); ful, rice dishes and grills are safe; baladi bread is everywhere but skippable.
Egypt.t: 'Nabati' = plant-based · Coptic fasting seasons make vegan food mainstream for weeks at a time.

Mauritius.v: Huge Indian heritage = vegetarian paradise: dholl puri, gateau piment, seven-curries thali are all veg by default.
Mauritius.g: Dholl puri wraps are wheat; rice-based Creole curries and grilled fish are the GF lane.
Mauritius.t: 'Pena laviann' (Creole) = no meat · temple canteens serve superb cheap veg thali.

Spain.v: Tortilla, gazpacho, salmorejo (check bread), pimientos de padrón, escalivada — tapas culture has a veg lane if you order à la carte.
Spain.g: Jamón, tortilla, grilled fish are GF; beware croquetas (flour) and always ask about 'harina' in sauces. GF menus are legally common.
Spain.t: 'Soy celiaco/a' is widely understood — Spain is one of Europe's best coeliac countries.

Italy.v: Pasta al pomodoro, pizza marinara, contorni (side vegetables), and the whole aperitivo spread — vegetarian Italy is effortless; vegan needs 'senza formaggio'.
Italy.g: The pasta country is also a coeliac leader: 'senza glutine' pizza and pasta are certified (look for AIC signs) in most cities.
Italy.t: 'Senza glutine' · 'vegano' is understood everywhere north of clichés.

France.v: Classic bistros are stubborn, but boulangerie salads, falafel (Paris Marais!), and modern néo-bistros carry you; cheese makes vegetarian easy, vegan harder.
France.g: Galettes (buckwheat crêpes) are the great naturally-GF French meal; 'sans gluten' bakeries thrive in Paris.
France.t: 'Sans gluten' / 'végétalien' (vegan) — say it with confidence, get a shrug, get fed anyway.

Belgium.v: Frites are traditionally beef-fat fried — ask 'végétal?'; Ghent invented the weekly veggie day and Brussels has serious vegan frites.
Belgium.g: Mussels and most frites are GF (check fryer); waffles and beer are the wheat walls — GF beer exists in specialist bars.
Belgium.t: 'Veggie dag' culture means every town has at least one full veggie kitchen.

United Kingdom.v: The UK is Europe's vegan-label champion — every supermarket, pub and chippy has marked options; haggis comes in a beloved veggie version.
United Kingdom.g: GF is legally labeled everywhere; chippies increasingly run dedicated GF fryers (check the sign).
United Kingdom.t: Just read the label — UK menus mark V, VG and GF as standard.

Portugal.v: Traditional menus are fish-heavy; vegetarians live well on soups (check stock), tomato rice and Lisbon's modern veg scene.
Portugal.g: Grilled fish + rice + salad is the national GF meal; pastel de nata is wheat, alas.
Portugal.t: 'Sem glúten' · 'vegetariano' — Lisbon and Porto both have full vegan quarters now.

Norway.v: Supermarkets are your ally: excellent plant-based ranges; restaurant menus always carry at least one veg dish, often superb.
Norway.g: Fish, potatoes and root veg are the traditional GF core; 'glutenfri' labeling is universal and reliable.
Norway.t: Allergy law is strict — staff can list every allergen from memory. Just ask.

Sweden.v: Possibly Europe's easiest vegan country per capita — oat-milk homeland, and every lunch buffet has a green option.
Sweden.g: 'Glutenfri' is labeled by law; knäckebröd traps aside, GF bread is in every ICA.
Sweden.t: Say nothing — just read the menu icons. Sweden did the work already.

Finland.v: Helsinki's lounas buffets almost always include a vegan pot; oat everything, everywhere.
Finland.g: Rye is the national grain — GF options are labeled ('gluteeniton') and common; Karelian pasties come GF in bigger shops.
Finland.t: 'Kasvis' = veg · 'vegaani' = vegan · allergy literacy is total.

Czechia.v: Beyond fried cheese: Prague has one of Central Europe's biggest vegan scenes; traditional menus offer smažený sýr and dumplings-with-sauce vegetarian picks.
Czechia.g: Dumplings and beer are wheat; roast meats + potatoes are safe. 'Bezlepkové' menus appear in most Prague districts.
Czechia.t: 'Bez masa' = meat-free · Prague's vegan map is genuinely long.

Slovakia.v: Bryndzové halušky is vegetarian (sheep cheese); fasting-food tradition helps vegans in rural spots; Bratislava has modern veg bistros.
Slovakia.g: Halušky are potato-flour based but check; grills + potato dishes are the safe rail.

Romania.v: Orthodox fasting ('de post') menus are vegan by definition — zacuscă, fasole bătută, sarmale de post; every menu marks them.
Romania.g: Mămăliga (polenta) is the great GF staple; covrigi and bread are the wheat.
Romania.t: 'De post' = fasting = plant-based — Romania's menus label it as a category.

Poland.v: Warsaw and Gdańsk rank among Europe's top vegan cities; pierogi ruskie are vegetarian and milk bars always have meatless classics.
Poland.g: Pierogi are wheat; placki ziemniaczane (potato pancakes) and grilled dishes are safer; 'bezglutenowe' labeling is growing fast.
Poland.t: 'Jarskie' = meatless — the milk-bar word to know.

Estonia.v: Tallinn's Telliskivi quarter is wall-to-wall plant-based; traditional menus always carry mushroom and potato mains.
Estonia.g: Black rye bread is the icon and the trap; otherwise fish + potato culture is GF-friendly and labeling is exact.
Estonia.t: 'Taimne' = plant-based · Bolt Food filters by diet if it's raining.

Latvia.v: Riga Central Market solves everything: berries, pickles, hemp butter, grey peas (vegan national dish!).
Latvia.g: Grey peas with (skip the) speck, potato dishes and fish are GF; rye bread is the wheat wall.
Latvia.t: 'Bez gaļas' = without meat · grey peas + kefir is the original Latvian plant bowl.

United States.v: Miami's Cuban counters do beans-rice-plantains vegan by accident; every US city menu marks V/VG and delivery apps filter by diet.
United States.g: GF is a mainstream menu category — dedicated fryers and GF buns are normal in Florida chains.
United States.t: Just ask — US servers recite allergens like poetry.

Dominican Republic.v: Mangú, tostones, rice-and-beans, avocado — the Dominican plate goes plant-based easily if you ask 'sin carne'.
Dominican Republic.g: Plantain and rice culture = naturally GF core; watch fried items sharing oil with breaded things.
Dominican Republic.t: 'Sin gluten' at resorts is well handled — buffets label; in comedores, point and smile.

visa.general: For most short tourist trips, citizens of the US, UK, EU/Schengen, Canada, Australia and New Zealand either enter visa-free or get a simple online authorisation (an eVisa or eTA) before flying. Typical visa-free stays run 30–90 days. Some countries want a visa arranged in advance, and a growing number ask you to fill an online arrival or eVisa form even when 'visa-free' — so always check the official portal for your exact nationality before you book.
visa.schengen: This is a Schengen-area country. Most US, UK, EU, Canadian, Australian, NZ, Brazilian, Japanese and Korean passports enter visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period across the whole Schengen zone. From 2025 the EU's ETIAS pre-authorisation applies to visa-free non-EU visitors — check before you fly.
